questions.question: A lava flow pours across one forest and hardens into new rock. A wildfire burns another forest down to blackened stumps. Ecologists call the regrowth on the lava primary succession, and the regrowth after the fire secondary succession. What decides which kind it is?
questions.answer: Whether there is soil left for plants to root in
choices: Whether there is soil left for plants to root in
Whether the plants that come back match the old ones
How hot the ground grows while it happens
How wide an area of land it lays bare
questions.context: Primary succession starts where there is no soil at all: fresh lava, rock scraped bare by a glacier, a new island. A fire, however hot, leaves the soil in place with seeds, roots and nutrients in it, so the regrowth after it is secondary and much faster. Cold rock left by a melting glacier starts primary succession too, so heat is not what decides.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.12B, map line G8.L5) teaches primary succession on new ground with no soil and secondary succession after a disturbance that leaves the soil.

questions.question: A grey crust of lichen spreads across a bare granite boulder that a glacier has left behind, long before any plant can grow there. Over many years a thin film of soil gathers around it, and mosses begin to grow in it. How does the lichen begin to turn the rock into soil?
questions.answer: Acids it gives off eat away at the rock's surface
choices: Acids it gives off eat away at the rock's surface
Oxygen it gives off rusts the rock's surface away
Salt it gathers from the rain crumbles the rock
Rain it soaks up softens the rock into mud
questions.context: A lichen has no roots and drinks from rain, dew and damp air, and its fungus gives off acids, such as oxalic acid, that break down the minerals of the rock. Loosened rock grains mix with the remains of dead lichens into the first thin soil, where mosses can take hold. The rock already sits in air that is a fifth oxygen, so the little a lichen gives off changes nothing, and rain alone wears granite down far more slowly than a lichen's acids do.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L5) teaches that pioneer species such as lichens slowly build soil on bare rock; how they do it, with acids that weather the rock, is the grade's mechanism.

questions.question: A cotton field in the Piedmont of North Carolina is left to grow wild. Horseweed covers it the first summer and asters the next, then broomsedge grass, and within about twenty years young pines stand over it. Over the next century, hardwood trees such as oaks and hickories take the pines' place. What lets the hardwoods do it?
questions.answer: Their seedlings can grow in shade that young pines cannot
choices: Their seedlings can grow in shade that young pines cannot
Their seedlings outgrow young pines in bright sunlight
Their roots give off a poison that kills the pines
The pines all die of old age by about forty years
questions.context: In the bright sun of an open field, pines grow faster than oaks and hickories, so they make the first forest. Their shade then keeps most young pines from growing beneath them, while shade-tolerant hardwood seedlings grow up there, ready to fill each gap as the old pines die at 80 to 120 years. Shade does the work, not poison, and the field becomes a hardwood forest in a century or two.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L5) teaches secondary succession on an abandoned farm field; why one stage gives way to the next is the grade's mechanism.

questions.question: Henry Chandler Cowles walked inland from the shore of Lake Michigan in the 1890s, across dune after dune. Beach grass grew on the dunes nearest the water. Farther back stood cottonwoods, then pines, and on the dunes farthest from the lake, an oak forest. What did Cowles conclude these bands of plants were?
questions.answer: Stages that a young dune passes through over time
choices: Stages that a young dune passes through over time
Separate groups, each kept to its own kind of sand
Separate groups, each kept to its own climate
Remains of one forest that the lake wind cut back
questions.context: The lake built its dunes one after another as the shore moved out, so the dunes farthest inland were the oldest. Cowles read the line of communities in space as a line in time: given the centuries, a beach-grass dune would hold cottonwoods, then pines and at last oaks, each community building the soil for the next. His study, published in 1899, helped found the idea of primary succession.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade lessons on succession tell how it was first read from dunes of different ages; Cowles's dunes are the classic case of primary succession.

questions.question: Mount St. Helens erupted in May 1980. On some of the ground it laid waste, green plants were growing again that same summer. On other ground close by, no plant grew that first summer, and parts of it were still almost bare decades later. What did the quicker ground have that the slower ground lacked?
questions.answer: Plants and roots that had lived through the blast
choices: Plants and roots that had lived through the blast
Sunlight on the ground where the trees had fallen
Warmth the eruption had left in the ground
A thicker blanket of fresh volcanic ash
questions.context: The quicker ground was forest flattened by the blast: late snow had sheltered some plants, others lived on as roots in the soil among the fallen trees, and pocket gophers lived through it in their burrows, so it grew back as in secondary succession. The slower ground lay under 3 to 12 metres of pumice from flows of hot rock, which held their heat for weeks and left nothing alive, so it had to start almost from nothing, as in primary succession, though it lay as open to the sun. Even there a prairie lupine took root within about a year, and its dead stems and leaves began a seedbed for other plants.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.12B) teaches why succession goes faster where a disturbance leaves soil and survivors; Mount St. Helens is the standard modern case.

questions.question: Surtsey rose out of the sea off Iceland in an eruption that began in 1963, and only a few scientists may land on it, so that life can reach it unaided. For some twenty years only about ten kinds of plants took hold on its bare lava and ash. Then gulls began to nest there, and inside their colony plants spread thickly and many new kinds took root, while the ground outside stayed almost bare. What did the gulls give the plants?
questions.answer: Nutrients from the sea, in their droppings
choices: Nutrients from the sea, in their droppings
Shelter from the wind, among their nests
Protection from the insects they hunt
Warmth from their bodies as they nest
questions.context: Gulls feed at sea and leave their droppings and pellets on land, rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, the nutrients that bare lava and ash lack. Inside the colony plant cover, the number of species and the soil all grew far faster than on the ground outside, which stayed barren. Birds also carried in seeds, but ecologists who study the island name the nutrients the birds bring from sea to land as the main force behind its new ecosystem.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L5) teaches primary succession on new land; an island watched from its birth shows what holds succession back and what speeds it.

questions.question: Frederic Clements argued in his book Plant Succession, in 1916, that in each climate succession always ends in one final community, the climax, which then holds steady. He likened a plant community to an organism that is born, grows and matures. How do most ecologists see a climax community today?
questions.answer: Less fixed than he thought, since fires and storms reset it
choices: Less fixed than he thought, since fires and storms reset it
Just as he said, one fixed end point for each climate
A myth, since communities change at random with no pattern
Fixed, but one for each kind of soil, not each climate
questions.context: Ecologists have largely given up the idea of one steady climax for each climate, because fires, storms, floods and chance keep knocking patches of land back to earlier stages; a landscape is a patchwork of stages, yet succession is not random either, for its stages follow real patterns. Arthur Tansley's polyclimax of 1935 allowed several climaxes in one climate, set by soil, slope, fire and grazing, but each still a fixed end point. Henry Gleason challenged Clements from 1917, and in 1926 called a plant community a coincidence rather than an organism.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade lessons carry succession toward a stable climax community; the honest modern caveat, that a climax is less fixed than Clements thought, belongs with it.

questions.question: Ground left bare by a melting glacier holds only crusts of lichen and moss at first. Over the next two centuries shrubs move in, and at last a forest grows there. Far more kinds of insects and birds live in the forest than ever lived among the mosses. Why do so many more kinds live there?
questions.answer: Its layers of plants give more kinds of food and shelter
choices: Its layers of plants give more kinds of food and shelter
Its animals have had time to evolve into new kinds
Its trees give off the oxygen that the animals need
Its trees make food from sunlight, which mosses cannot
questions.context: A forest has tall trees, smaller trees, shrubs and plants on its floor, over deep soil, and each layer offers its own food and hiding places, so many more kinds of animals can each find a living. The new kinds move in from the country around as the layers build up; they do not evolve on the spot. Mosses make their own food from sunlight just as trees do, and the air over a moss field holds as much oxygen as the air in a forest.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.12B) teaches how species diversity changes as succession goes on.

questions.question: Lichens and mosses are the first to cover a new lava flow. Over the centuries that follow, grasses take root among them, then shrubs, and at last trees. What lets each bigger kind of plant move in?
questions.answer: Each stage leaves deeper soil as it dies and rots
choices: Each stage leaves deeper soil as it dies and rots
Each stage lets more sunlight reach the ground
The lava's surface takes centuries to cool down
The insects that eat seedlings slowly die out
questions.context: As each generation of plants dies and rots, its remains add to the soil, which grows deeper and richer over the years. Deeper soil holds the water and nutrients that the bigger roots of grasses, then shrubs, then trees need, and each new stage casts more shade than the last, not less. A lava surface cools far sooner than that: lichens grew on Surtsey's lava three years after its eruption ended.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.L5) teaches that pioneers slowly build soil and are followed by grasses, shrubs and trees; how each stage readies the ground for the next is the mechanism.

44dcb8ec7d.why: Judge (medium): heat from a thin crust and the crust's weight were not live for an 8th grader. They are replaced by 'Oxygen it gives off rusts the rock's surface away' (a real confusion: the lichen's green partner does give off oxygen, but the rock already sits in air that is a fifth oxygen, F25, and lichens weather rock with acids, F5) and the judge's 'Rain it soaks up softens the rock into mud'. The judge's 'roots grow into cracks' was not used: a lichen has no roots, but its threads do reach into rock, so that choice was partly true. The key now shares its 'it gives off' form with a wrong choice. Stem and key unchanged; the context answers the two new choices.

a480b07ae6.why: Judge (medium): 'Fixed, but found only in forests and never elsewhere' was weak, leaving the moderate key standing. It is replaced by Tansley's polyclimax of 1935 as a second, respectable revision: 'Fixed, but one for each kind of soil, not each climate' (F27), wrong because ecologists now doubt fixed end points at all (F23). Fact-check (error): the context now says Gleason challenged Clements from 1917 and in 1926 called a plant community a coincidence (F22, F26). Stem and key unchanged.

67c98e9246.why: Judge (medium): the key alone echoed the stem's 'kinds' and alone explained variety, and the hawk-and-owl choice was weak. The hawk-and-owl choice is replaced by 'Its animals have had time to evolve into new kinds', the grade's real confusion of succession with evolution: it explains variety too and shares the word 'kinds', so the key is no longer the only choice about kinds. It is wrong because new species arrive from the country around as succession goes on (F24, F30). Stem and key unchanged; the context answers the new choice.

0dd1589835.why: Judge (high): the stem's own description of the two zones ruled out every wrong choice (the pumice plain was open, hot and deeply buried too). The judge's rebuild (where most of the first plants came from) was not used: USGS says wind-dispersed herbs colonized the blast zone's bare surfaces in the first year and dominated many areas within 4 to 7 years, so 'seeds blown in' was partly true. The stem now gives only the outcome (plants that same summer on one ground, none for two years on the other, F16, F18, F28), so sunlight, leftover warmth and a thicker ash blanket stay live; each is wrong (both grounds lay open; the pumice held its heat for weeks and lay 3 to 12 metres deep, F28). Key unchanged.

dropped.question: William Cooper marked out small plots at Glacier Bay, Alaska, in 1916, on ground the retreating ice had just left bare, and he and later ecologists came back to count their plants for a century. Each plot was expected to pass from mosses and low shrubs to willows, then alders, then spruce forest. Willows moved into many plots in the 1920s and are still there, while alder and spruce are scarce. What does the long count suggest?
dropped.why: Judge (high): 'Willows are the final stage of succession there' fits the stem's data as well as the key, and the key (early arrivals keep later ones out) is college ecology. The lead's re-aims did not survive the sources: Buma's team found species richness rose over the century while the effective number of species fell under the willows (F29), so a diversity key has two honest answers; their 2019 paper found 'no predictable species sequence or timeline', so a how-long key is not safe either; and which plants come first is already asked by 44dcb8ec7d and a3323c7e2e. The unit's scope is covered by its other nine questions.
